articles.title: Left 4 Dead 2 Dev Admits Valve Intentionally Leaked Its Own Trailer After the ESRB Blocked It from Release
articles.description: Former Valve writer Chet Faliszek has a confession to make: Valve intentionally leaked its own Left 4 Dead 2 trailer.

h1: Left 4 Dead 2 Dev Admits Valve Intentionally Leaked Its Own Trailer After the ESRB Blocked It from Release

contentBlocks.text: Former Valve writer Chet Faliszek has a confession to make: Valve intentionally leaked its own Left 4 Dead 2 trailer.

The Half-Life and Portal veteran spilled the beans on the studio's past unconventional marketing tactics in a new video uploaded to his YouTube channel (via Ars Technica ). Based on his recounting of the Left 4 Dead 2 incident, Valve "leaked our trailer ahead of time because" the Entertainment Software Rating Board (ESRB) "wouldn't let us release the trailer."
So, why are we just hearing about this now? Well, it's been a few years since any of this would have mattered.

"I think we can't get in trouble for that now. It was like 20 years ago," Faliszek said. "It's funny seeing leaked stuff now because, yeah, I don't think you can look for 'leaked Left 4 Dead 2 trailer' because it's just going to be lost."

Leaks can happen for a variety of reasons. Sometimes companies are hacked and have their content spilled out onto the internet ; sometimes someone says something they shouldn't , and sometimes materials are mistakenly published early . Most developers and publishers have their own process to ensure leaks don't happen, but in the case of Left 4 Dead 2, Valve saw opportunity.

The leaked footage in question appears to be the Zombie Survival Guide cinematic trailer , which maybe not-so-mysteriously appeared online in October 2009, one month before the launch of Left 4 Dead 2. It's a three-minute story video that lets survivors Coach, Ellis, Nick, and Rochelle loose to tear through hordes of zombies with chainsaws, guns, and more. Although it's quite violent, Faliszek didn't say exactly what the ESRB had taken issue with. Whatever it was, it didn't seem to matter much to Valve.

"Yeah, it originally got leaked because we had this with the ESRB, so that's why a lot of the language had to get toned down," he continued.

It all certainly seemed to work out for the best – at least for Valve. Left 4 Dead 2 went on to launch to rave reviews from critics and fans, including a 9/10 review from IGN. Although it never led to a third game (because of course it didn't), we found a lot to love about the multiplayer zombie sequel, calling it "one of the most distinctive co-operative titles out there" at the time.

articles.title: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke
articles.description: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

h1: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke

contentBlocks.text: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

If you thought the launch trailer for the PlayStation 5-exclusive video game would come and go without controversy, I've got bad news. Despite coming in at a little less than a minute and a half long, Marvel's Wolverine managed to kick up a storm of confusion online after fans spotted what they believed was a new character wielding a familiar-looking purple energy sword.

In comments across YouTube, Instagram, X/Twitter, and other social media platforms, you don't have to look too hard to find watchers questioning if the sneering villain featured in the launch trailer was Psylocke. Psylocke is an energy-wielding mutant who's been known to show up across various X-Men stories in the past, so when a glowing sword showed up in Marvel's Wolverine, many believed it to be tied to a grand character reveal.
Well, it's not, and Insomniac has done its best to make that clear.
Deathstrike. #WolverinePS5 pic.twitter.com/koWhS5v3HG

The post above was published earlier today and labels the sword user as Lady Deathstrike. The PlayStation developer didn't outright say it's trying to quiet the noise that's emerged in the days following the trailer's reveal, but judging by the comments, many are shocked any clarification was needed in the first place.
"The fact it has to be stated is so crazy to me," one user said . "Larp monsters are everywhere."
"No that’s Psylocke, some guy told me and he’s for sure right," another user joked .

It really does seem to be the purple sword that's to blame here because, as some have noted, Lady Deathstrike looks nothing like Psylocke. The version of the character featured in Marvel's Wolverine doesn't exactly have a comic-accurate design, but her vest and hair do more to link her to Lady Deathstrike than the character many were making her out to be.

There's also the fact that Insomniac has talked about Lady Deathstrike being in Marvel's Wolverine before, with the launch trailer also being far from the first time we've even seen her in the game. For example, one early look at her new design arrived in July's Ain't No Hero trailer , while a GIF the studio posted on social media showed her looking down on viewers.

These aren't clips of her doing anything you'd expect Psylocke to do either. This version has been shown attacking Logan with Lady Deathstrike's instantly recognizable finger claws on full display multiple times. Why she's using that sword or where it came from remains a mystery, but whatever the reason, it's not because she's actually Psylocke. That's not to say that character isn't in the game at all; other X-Men regulars like Jean Grey and Sabretooth are confirmed to make an apperance. If Psylockie is in the game, though, Insomniac hasn't publicly said a thing about her.

Logan will at least take on Lady Deathstrike – not Psylocke – when Marvel's Wolverine launches for PS5 September 15, 2026. Meanwhile, the launch trailer actually arrived as part of a recent State of Play presentation from Sony, which you can catch up on here . articles.title: Zach Cregger Says He's Done With Franchise Films After Resident Evil
articles.description: Resident Evil movie director Zach Cregger is days away from his survival horror adaptation's theatrical premiere, but don't expect him to help bring another franchise film to the big screen ever again.

h1: Zach Cregger Says He's Done With Franchise Films After Resident Evil
h2: "I’m doing this, and that’s it for me."

contentBlocks.text: Resident Evil movie director Zach Cregger is days away from his survival horror adaptation's theatrical premiere, but don't expect him to help bring another franchise film to the big screen ever again.

The filmmaker behind this month's Capcom project talked about what's next for him during a conversation with Deadline . When asked if he's ever been pressured to spearhead another recognizable IP, he gave a blunt answer: "I'm not doing that."

"I have never been approached by another franchise," Cregger said. "Maybe I have, but it would never get to me because I have been very clear that I’m not doing that. I’m doing this, and that’s it for me."

One might suspect Cregger's aversion to big franchise films like Resident Evil might stem from the backlash he's received in the months leading up to his movie's premiere. While the Barbarian and Weapons creator certainly has plenty of defenders looking forward to seeing his new live-action take, there have been many, many others who aren't quite as excited.

Most of the pressure has come from those who feel his Resident Evil doesn't align with the game it's based on. Changes to the source material, including its modern setting and snowy Raccoon City , have set fans on edge, while others aren't in love with the idea of following a new protagonist (Austin Abrams' Bryan Hodukavich) instead of someone like Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield.

The controversy surrounding the Resident Evil movie has been quite loud , but there are several factors at play when it comes to his plans for the future. He clarified that the decision comes down to his status as a writer who wants "to write whatever I want to write."

"I don’t want to write something where I have to make sure I'm tagging different data points to satisfy X," he continued. "I just want to satisfy me. And the only reason that I think Resident Evil is OK for me to do is because I’m enthusiastic about the games and I like the story that I thought of with the games and I’m making it for me. I think this movie is cool, and I hope it checks the fan boxes because I’m a fan and I’m checking my boxes.
"I'm making the Resident Evil movie that I wish existed, so I can do that with a clean heart and a clear conscience and not feel like I’m getting f**ked by some weird industry thing."

Cregger has made it abundantly clear that his Resident Evil movie is meant to be a love letter to the experience of playing games like Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 7 and not a direct retelling of any one particular story. Although he's writing off franchise films in the future, it sounds like another trip to Raccoon City – or maybe even somewhere else in the Resident Evil universe – isn't out of the question yet. In another recent interview, the director said he already has "ideas" for a sequel , even if we have yet to see how audiences will respond to the first movie.
Resident Evil Movie Trailer Slideshow

Resident Evil is expected to have a big debut when it slithers into theaters September 18, 2026. Next up on his schedule are projects like the Siren Head movie , The Flood , and a Weapons prequel movie . While we wait to see Cregger's new vision for Raccoon City, you can check out a new trailer that revealed a sneak peek at a creature that looks suspiciously like RE4's Las Plagas . You can also check out its organ transplant bag-inspired popcorn bucket .
Photo by JC Olivera/Sony Pictures via Getty Images.

articles.title: ¡Kankichi Ryotsu vuelve a patrullar por Kameari! El mítico anime de Kochikame regresará en forma de remake
articles.description: Aunque One Piece sea famosa por ser extremadamente larga, no es ni de lejos la serie más extensa de Japón. Existe otro manga mitiquísimo que le supera por la derecha por bastante diferencia y que, tras casi una década desde su última aparición, regresará por todo lo alto el próximo año: Kochikame . A través de las cuentas oficiales de la serie y la Shonen Jump, la franquicia ha anunciado un remake completo del anime , empezando desde cero con un lavado de cara completo, desde actores y actrices de voz hasta estética y con una ventana de estreno en 2027. Eso sí, el estudio de animación será el mismo que el del anime que todos conocemos, aunque, eso sí, en manos de una nueva generación de artistas. Y si bien el anuncio ha sido altamente celebrado por los fans de Kankichi Ryotsu , lo cierto es que no se sabe con exactitud cómo será este remake, ya que, si pretenden hacer una adaptación del manga , tendrán que llevar a la pequeña pantalla la friolera cantidad de 2.000 capítulos . Y si bien parte del público tiene bastantes ganas, lo cierto es que durante los primeros meses de producción la gente estaba bastante escéptica por cómo iba a ser la película si se iba a alejar de todo lo que conocíamos. articles.title: El diseño de PS2 es uno de los más queridos por los fans de PlayStation, pero en realidad se lo debemos a un ordenador Atari de 1993
articles.description: Aquél monolito oscuro con letras degradadas, un logo que se giraba a placer, y un buen puñado de rendijas que se convirtieron en el lugar favorito de reposo de toda una generación de motas de polvo, no ha tardado en proclamarse como uno de los diseños más celebrados de la historia de las consolas. Teiyu Goto venía de diseñar la primera PlayStation y, para la segunda generación de consolas de Sony, decidió inspirarse en “ el vacío del espacio ” y el salto a una nueva dimensión de “ poder sin límites ” para crear el diseño de PS2 . Bueno, en eso y en un diseño de Atari que Sony compró. La semilla del diseño de PS2 Estamos en 1993, un año antes de que la primera PlayStation anime las navidades niponas. Al otro lado del charco, en la soleada California, la mítica Atari se prepara para otro lanzamiento que marcará un antes y un después en la industria del videojuego: Atari Jaguar . Normalmente lo de marcar un antes y un después suele ir atado a un éxito sin precedentes o un giro de 180º en la forma de hacer las cosas, pero en este caso lo que nos encontramos fue el último clavo sobre el ataúd de una Atari que lo había apostado todo a una carta, su éxito en el mundo de las consolas. Precisamente de esa apuesta germina esta historia, con la cancelación de la gama de ordenadores Atari para centrar el apoyo de la compañía en la Jaguar. Con dicha decisión, el abandono del proyecto que debía ser el siguiente paso de la compañía en el sector de los ordenadores personales, el prototipo Falcon 040 , queda en el limbo de los productos que no llegan a producción. La industria del PC le dice adiós antes de conocerlo al primer ordenador que puedes colocar en horizontal o en vertical . Una innovadora caja capaz de mantenerse en pie gracias a su diseño y un pedestal destinado a asegurar su estabilidad. Una idea que, tras guardarse en un cajón, quedaría aparcada durante los próximos siete años. En Vida Extra Por qué los discos de la primera PlayStation eran negros y los de PS2 eran azules De Atari a Sony Tras dar forma a no pocos televisores de la marca y sumarse al proyecto de PlayStation en el que crearía el diseño de la consola y sus mandos, incluyendo la iconografía del triángulo, el cuadrado, el círculo y la X -la simbología de un punto de vista, un trozo de papel, y las decisiones sí y no, respectivamente-, a Teiyu Goto le llega el reto de diseñar PS2 . Sobre el papel, un concepto que el propio diseñador aún mantiene entre sus logros más destacados en su página web : “ transmitir hacia el oscuro espacio exterior desde nuestro planeta de agua lleno de inteligencia ”. ¿El resultado? El clásico monolito negro con tintes azules que todos conocemos. Las comparaciones, como ya habréis podido comprobar por las imágenes, ceden hueco a mucho más que una bonita casualidad. Pese a los cambios estéticos, la similitud entre el ordenador de Atari y PS2 es más que evidente. Y lo es por razones justificadas, al menos a nivel legal, tal y como muestra esta patente . De aquella hecatombe que supuso el lanzamiento de Jaguar y la caída de Atari , Sony supo sacar tajada adquiriendo aquél diseño a la espera de darle una segunda vida. El mundo se quedó sin su Falcon 040, pero la suerte quiso que aquella idea volviese a la vida con el diseño de PS2 . contentBlocks.text: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless
Posted by Retromash
in Misc
Tagged with

Computer solitaire became memorable because it made a new machine feel understandable. A modern round on PlaySolitaire still uses the same essential visual language: a deck, clear columns, visible suits and cards that respond directly to the player. The technology around the game has changed dramatically, but the interaction remains immediate. That is why solitaire belongs in any conversation about the everyday design of classic computer games.

A deck became a lesson in mouse movement When Solitaire arrived with Windows 3.0 in 1990, many home computer users were still becoming comfortable with a mouse. Moving cards from one pile to another gave drag and drop a purpose that was easy to grasp. The player did not need to understand files, menus or commands. They only needed to recognise a card and place it where the rules allowed.

That was clever interface design disguised as a familiar pastime. The action on screen matched an action people already understood from the physical world. A card could be selected, moved and released. If the destination was wrong, the game refused the move. The feedback was simple and immediate.

The desktop game that needed little explanation Many early computer games had to teach players a new language. They introduced unfamiliar controls, icons and objectives at the same time. Solitaire avoided much of that work because the deck already carried meaning.

Red and black suits were easy to distinguish. Ordered columns showed progress. Empty spaces suggested possibility. The stock pile invited a click. Even a player who did not know every rule could experiment and learn from the response.

This made the game unusually approachable. It felt like software, but it did not feel technical. That balance helped it become part of the everyday computer rather than a special activity reserved for dedicated players.

Small interface choices built trust Classic solitaire interfaces were rarely spectacular. Their strength came from consistency. Cards stayed where they were placed. Legal moves behaved predictably. A completed sequence created a visible sense of order.

Those details built trust between the player and the machine. The computer was not hiding the rules or asking for a complicated input. It was maintaining the table, enforcing the structure and keeping score.

The same principle still matters in modern design. A good interface should make the next action feel obvious without making the result automatic. Solitaire achieves this with very little visual clutter. The player can see the problem, but solving it still requires attention.

Nostalgia is visual, but usability keeps it alive The green felt background and pixel card backs are powerful nostalgic images. They recall family computers, office breaks and the particular sound of a mouse button. Yet nostalgia alone does not explain why the game survives.

People return because the underlying interaction remains useful. A round starts quickly. Progress is visible. Failure is understandable. A new attempt creates a different arrangement without requiring a tutorial.

This is also why many attempts to modernise classic games go too far. Extra animations, reward systems and crowded menus can obscure the quality that made the original work. Solitaire does not need to pretend to be bigger than it is. Its modest scale is part of the appeal.

The browser is the new family computer The family computer once gathered software in a single physical place. Today, the browser performs a similar role across laptops, tablets and phones. It provides a common surface where a familiar game can appear without installation or a long setup process.

That shift changes access, but not the core experience. A card still needs a clear destination. A sequence still needs to be read. The player still chooses between an immediate move and a more patient plan.

Browser play also preserves another old habit: using a simple game as a boundary between tasks. One round can mark the end of work, fill a short wait or provide a calm reset before returning to something more demanding.

Why the old rhythm survives Computer solitaire lasts because its rhythm was never tied to one machine. It begins with disorder, asks for careful attention and rewards the gradual creation of structure. The interface supports that rhythm without getting in the way.

That is a useful lesson from classic software. Technology becomes memorable when it gives people a clear action, a reliable response and enough space to make their own decisions. Solitaire did that on the early desktop, and it continues to do it in the browser today.

selected.title: Left 4 Dead 2 Dev Admits Valve Intentionally Leaked Its Own Trailer After the ESRB Blocked It from Release
selected.description: Former Valve writer Chet Faliszek has a confession to make: Valve intentionally leaked its own Left 4 Dead 2 trailer.

h1: Left 4 Dead 2 Dev Admits Valve Intentionally Leaked Its Own Trailer After the ESRB Blocked It from Release

contentBlocks.text: Former Valve writer Chet Faliszek has a confession to make: Valve intentionally leaked its own Left 4 Dead 2 trailer.

The Half-Life and Portal veteran spilled the beans on the studio's past unconventional marketing tactics in a new video uploaded to his YouTube channel (via Ars Technica ). Based on his recounting of the Left 4 Dead 2 incident, Valve "leaked our trailer ahead of time because" the Entertainment Software Rating Board (ESRB) "wouldn't let us release the trailer."
So, why are we just hearing about this now? Well, it's been a few years since any of this would have mattered.

"I think we can't get in trouble for that now. It was like 20 years ago," Faliszek said. "It's funny seeing leaked stuff now because, yeah, I don't think you can look for 'leaked Left 4 Dead 2 trailer' because it's just going to be lost."

Leaks can happen for a variety of reasons. Sometimes companies are hacked and have their content spilled out onto the internet ; sometimes someone says something they shouldn't , and sometimes materials are mistakenly published early . Most developers and publishers have their own process to ensure leaks don't happen, but in the case of Left 4 Dead 2, Valve saw opportunity.

The leaked footage in question appears to be the Zombie Survival Guide cinematic trailer , which maybe not-so-mysteriously appeared online in October 2009, one month before the launch of Left 4 Dead 2. It's a three-minute story video that lets survivors Coach, Ellis, Nick, and Rochelle loose to tear through hordes of zombies with chainsaws, guns, and more. Although it's quite violent, Faliszek didn't say exactly what the ESRB had taken issue with. Whatever it was, it didn't seem to matter much to Valve.

"Yeah, it originally got leaked because we had this with the ESRB, so that's why a lot of the language had to get toned down," he continued.

It all certainly seemed to work out for the best – at least for Valve. Left 4 Dead 2 went on to launch to rave reviews from critics and fans, including a 9/10 review from IGN. Although it never led to a third game (because of course it didn't), we found a lot to love about the multiplayer zombie sequel, calling it "one of the most distinctive co-operative titles out there" at the time.
For more on Valve, you can check out our list of the top 10 best games the studio has made . You can also learn about the recent leak that has fans digging through more than a decade of files .

h2: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless

contentBlocks.text: The Interface Details That Made Computer Solitaire Feel Timeless
Posted by Retromash
in Misc
Tagged with

Computer solitaire became memorable because it made a new machine feel understandable. A modern round on PlaySolitaire still uses the same essential visual language: a deck, clear columns, visible suits and cards that respond directly to the player. The technology around the game has changed dramatically, but the interaction remains immediate. That is why solitaire belongs in any conversation about the everyday design of classic computer games.

A deck became a lesson in mouse movement When Solitaire arrived with Windows 3.0 in 1990, many home computer users were still becoming comfortable with a mouse. Moving cards from one pile to another gave drag and drop a purpose that was easy to grasp. The player did not need to understand files, menus or commands. They only needed to recognise a card and place it where the rules allowed.

That was clever interface design disguised as a familiar pastime. The action on screen matched an action people already understood from the physical world. A card could be selected, moved and released. If the destination was wrong, the game refused the move. The feedback was simple and immediate.

The desktop game that needed little explanation Many early computer games had to teach players a new language. They introduced unfamiliar controls, icons and objectives at the same time. Solitaire avoided much of that work because the deck already carried meaning.

Red and black suits were easy to distinguish. Ordered columns showed progress. Empty spaces suggested possibility. The stock pile invited a click. Even a player who did not know every rule could experiment and learn from the response.

This made the game unusually approachable. It felt like software, but it did not feel technical. That balance helped it become part of the everyday computer rather than a special activity reserved for dedicated players.

Small interface choices built trust Classic solitaire interfaces were rarely spectacular. Their strength came from consistency. Cards stayed where they were placed. Legal moves behaved predictably. A completed sequence created a visible sense of order.

Those details built trust between the player and the machine. The computer was not hiding the rules or asking for a complicated input. It was maintaining the table, enforcing the structure and keeping score.

The same principle still matters in modern design. A good interface should make the next action feel obvious without making the result automatic. Solitaire achieves this with very little visual clutter. The player can see the problem, but solving it still requires attention.

Nostalgia is visual, but usability keeps it alive The green felt background and pixel card backs are powerful nostalgic images. They recall family computers, office breaks and the particular sound of a mouse button. Yet nostalgia alone does not explain why the game survives.

People return because the underlying interaction remains useful. A round starts quickly. Progress is visible. Failure is understandable. A new attempt creates a different arrangement without requiring a tutorial.

This is also why many attempts to modernise classic games go too far. Extra animations, reward systems and crowded menus can obscure the quality that made the original work. Solitaire does not need to pretend to be bigger than it is. Its modest scale is part of the appeal.

The browser is the new family computer The family computer once gathered software in a single physical place. Today, the browser performs a similar role across laptops, tablets and phones. It provides a common surface where a familiar game can appear without installation or a long setup process.

That shift changes access, but not the core experience. A card still needs a clear destination. A sequence still needs to be read. The player still chooses between an immediate move and a more patient plan.

Browser play also preserves another old habit: using a simple game as a boundary between tasks. One round can mark the end of work, fill a short wait or provide a calm reset before returning to something more demanding.

Why the old rhythm survives Computer solitaire lasts because its rhythm was never tied to one machine. It begins with disorder, asks for careful attention and rewards the gradual creation of structure. The interface supports that rhythm without getting in the way.

That is a useful lesson from classic software. Technology becomes memorable when it gives people a clear action, a reliable response and enough space to make their own decisions. Solitaire did that on the early desktop, and it continues to do it in the browser today.

selected.title: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke
selected.description: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

h1: Insomniac Clears the Air After Marvel's Wolverine Fans Confuse Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke

contentBlocks.text: Insomniac Games has cleared the air after a new trailer for Marvel's Wolverine had fans confusing Lady Deathstrike for Psylocke.

If you thought the launch trailer for the PlayStation 5-exclusive video game would come and go without controversy, I've got bad news. Despite coming in at a little less than a minute and a half long, Marvel's Wolverine managed to kick up a storm of confusion online after fans spotted what they believed was a new character wielding a familiar-looking purple energy sword.

In comments across YouTube, Instagram, X/Twitter, and other social media platforms, you don't have to look too hard to find watchers questioning if the sneering villain featured in the launch trailer was Psylocke. Psylocke is an energy-wielding mutant who's been known to show up across various X-Men stories in the past, so when a glowing sword showed up in Marvel's Wolverine, many believed it to be tied to a grand character reveal.
Well, it's not, and Insomniac has done its best to make that clear.
Deathstrike. #WolverinePS5 pic.twitter.com/koWhS5v3HG

The post above was published earlier today and labels the sword user as Lady Deathstrike. The PlayStation developer didn't outright say it's trying to quiet the noise that's emerged in the days following the trailer's reveal, but judging by the comments, many are shocked any clarification was needed in the first place.
"The fact it has to be stated is so crazy to me," one user said . "Larp monsters are everywhere."
"No that’s Psylocke, some guy told me and he’s for sure right," another user joked .

It really does seem to be the purple sword that's to blame here because, as some have noted, Lady Deathstrike looks nothing like Psylocke. The version of the character featured in Marvel's Wolverine doesn't exactly have a comic-accurate design, but her vest and hair do more to link her to Lady Deathstrike than the character many were making her out to be.

There's also the fact that Insomniac has talked about Lady Deathstrike being in Marvel's Wolverine before, with the launch trailer also being far from the first time we've even seen her in the game. For example, one early look at her new design arrived in July's Ain't No Hero trailer , while a GIF the studio posted on social media showed her looking down on viewers.

These aren't clips of her doing anything you'd expect Psylocke to do either. This version has been shown attacking Logan with Lady Deathstrike's instantly recognizable finger claws on full display multiple times. Why she's using that sword or where it came from remains a mystery, but whatever the reason, it's not because she's actually Psylocke. That's not to say that character isn't in the game at all; other X-Men regulars like Jean Grey and Sabretooth are confirmed to make an apperance. If Psylockie is in the game, though, Insomniac hasn't publicly said a thing about her.

Logan will at least take on Lady Deathstrike – not Psylocke – when Marvel's Wolverine launches for PS5 September 15, 2026. Meanwhile, the launch trailer actually arrived as part of a recent State of Play presentation from Sony, which you can catch up on here . For more, you can check out IGN's last full preview and our breakdown for the game's many, many suits .

selected.title: "Fui muy ingenuo": el director de la película de Resident Evil pensaba que los fans no se iban a enfadar con los cambios de la nueva adaptación
selected.description: En tan solo dos semanas, Capcom volverá a los cines de todo el mundo con la nueva adaptación de Resident Evil , una que se alejará por completo no solo de las películas anteriores, sino de cualquier cosa vista en la franquicia, incluidos los videojuegos que se han ido lanzando desde hace 30 años. Y si bien parte del público tiene bastantes ganas, lo cierto es que durante los primeros meses de producción la gente estaba bastante escéptica por cómo iba a ser la película si se iba a alejar de todo lo que conocíamos. Sobre esto ha hablado el propio Zach Cregger , que, en una entrevista con IGN , reconoció ser un ingenuo al pensar que los fans no se iban a molestar. "Creo que fui muy ingenuo. Pensaba que los fans de estos juegos, como yo, estarían encantados de que alguien viniera y convirtiera Resident Evil en una película de survival horror. Yo pensaba: "Genial". No entendí realmente ese sentimiento de: "Llevamos muchísimo tiempo esperando la historia de Leon". Lo entiendo, y siento que esa no sea la historia que estoy contando. Comprendo la frustración. Lo entiendo perfectamente porque no he visto las películas anteriores de Resident Evil, porque no se parecen al Resident Evil que a mí me encanta, así que ¿cómo podría enfadarme con los fans que tienen esa misma actitud?". En Vida Extra Square Enix no está en venta. Entonces, ¿por qué un fondo ya tiene casi el 20% y vuelve a hablarse de una compra? Cregger explica que su forma de ver Resident Evil no era precisamente la historia de Leon o Claire, sino lo que puede llegar a transmitir la saga. Al final, lo que Cregger quiere transmitir de la saga no es la historia del Virus T , sino las sensaciones que nos deja la saga al jugar. Es por ello que veremos escenas en primera o tercera persona, así como una visión clara de la gestión de recursos para saber en todo momento qué munición tiene nuestro personaje. El cineasta menciona que entiende el enfado de parte de la comunidad, pero que, al fin y al cabo, su forma de ver la saga no está en los personajes o la historia, sino en su ambientación, inmersión y jugabilidad. selected.title: Zach Cregger Says He's Done With Franchise Films After Resident Evil
selected.description: Resident Evil movie director Zach Cregger is days away from his survival horror adaptation's theatrical premiere, but don't expect him to help bring another franchise film to the big screen ever again.

h1: Zach Cregger Says He's Done With Franchise Films After Resident Evil
h2: "I’m doing this, and that’s it for me."

contentBlocks.text: Resident Evil movie director Zach Cregger is days away from his survival horror adaptation's theatrical premiere, but don't expect him to help bring another franchise film to the big screen ever again.

The filmmaker behind this month's Capcom project talked about what's next for him during a conversation with Deadline . When asked if he's ever been pressured to spearhead another recognizable IP, he gave a blunt answer: "I'm not doing that."

"I have never been approached by another franchise," Cregger said. "Maybe I have, but it would never get to me because I have been very clear that I’m not doing that. I’m doing this, and that’s it for me."

One might suspect Cregger's aversion to big franchise films like Resident Evil might stem from the backlash he's received in the months leading up to his movie's premiere. While the Barbarian and Weapons creator certainly has plenty of defenders looking forward to seeing his new live-action take, there have been many, many others who aren't quite as excited.

Most of the pressure has come from those who feel his Resident Evil doesn't align with the game it's based on. Changes to the source material, including its modern setting and snowy Raccoon City , have set fans on edge, while others aren't in love with the idea of following a new protagonist (Austin Abrams' Bryan Hodukavich) instead of someone like Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield.

The controversy surrounding the Resident Evil movie has been quite loud , but there are several factors at play when it comes to his plans for the future. He clarified that the decision comes down to his status as a writer who wants "to write whatever I want to write."

"I don’t want to write something where I have to make sure I'm tagging different data points to satisfy X," he continued. "I just want to satisfy me. And the only reason that I think Resident Evil is OK for me to do is because I’m enthusiastic about the games and I like the story that I thought of with the games and I’m making it for me. I think this movie is cool, and I hope it checks the fan boxes because I’m a fan and I’m checking my boxes.
"I'm making the Resident Evil movie that I wish existed, so I can do that with a clean heart and a clear conscience and not feel like I’m getting f**ked by some weird industry thing."

Cregger has made it abundantly clear that his Resident Evil movie is meant to be a love letter to the experience of playing games like Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 7 and not a direct retelling of any one particular story. Although he's writing off franchise films in the future, it sounds like another trip to Raccoon City – or maybe even somewhere else in the Resident Evil universe – isn't out of the question yet. In another recent interview, the director said he already has "ideas" for a sequel , even if we have yet to see how audiences will respond to the first movie.
Resident Evil Movie Trailer Slideshow

Resident Evil is expected to have a big debut when it slithers into theaters September 18, 2026. Next up on his schedule are projects like the Siren Head movie , The Flood , and a Weapons prequel movie . While we wait to see Cregger's new vision for Raccoon City, you can check out a new trailer that revealed a sneak peek at a creature that looks suspiciously like RE4's Las Plagas . You can also check out its organ transplant bag-inspired popcorn bucket .
Photo by JC Olivera/Sony Pictures via Getty Images.

selected.title: El diseño de PS2 es uno de los más queridos por los fans de PlayStation, pero en realidad se lo debemos a un ordenador Atari de 1993
selected.description: Aquél monolito oscuro con letras degradadas, un logo que se giraba a placer, y un buen puñado de rendijas que se convirtieron en el lugar favorito de reposo de toda una generación de motas de polvo, no ha tardado en proclamarse como uno de los diseños más celebrados de la historia de las consolas. Teiyu Goto venía de diseñar la primera PlayStation y, para la segunda generación de consolas de Sony, decidió inspirarse en “ el vacío del espacio ” y el salto a una nueva dimensión de “ poder sin límites ” para crear el diseño de PS2 . Bueno, en eso y en un diseño de Atari que Sony compró. La semilla del diseño de PS2 Estamos en 1993, un año antes de que la primera PlayStation anime las navidades niponas. Al otro lado del charco, en la soleada California, la mítica Atari se prepara para otro lanzamiento que marcará un antes y un después en la industria del videojuego: Atari Jaguar . Normalmente lo de marcar un antes y un después suele ir atado a un éxito sin precedentes o un giro de 180º en la forma de hacer las cosas, pero en este caso lo que nos encontramos fue el último clavo sobre el ataúd de una Atari que lo había apostado todo a una carta, su éxito en el mundo de las consolas. Precisamente de esa apuesta germina esta historia, con la cancelación de la gama de ordenadores Atari para centrar el apoyo de la compañía en la Jaguar. Con dicha decisión, el abandono del proyecto que debía ser el siguiente paso de la compañía en el sector de los ordenadores personales, el prototipo Falcon 040 , queda en el limbo de los productos que no llegan a producción. La industria del PC le dice adiós antes de conocerlo al primer ordenador que puedes colocar en horizontal o en vertical . Una innovadora caja capaz de mantenerse en pie gracias a su diseño y un pedestal destinado a asegurar su estabilidad. Una idea que, tras guardarse en un cajón, quedaría aparcada durante los próximos siete años. En Vida Extra Por qué los discos de la primera PlayStation eran negros y los de PS2 eran azules De Atari a Sony Tras dar forma a no pocos televisores de la marca y sumarse al proyecto de PlayStation en el que crearía el diseño de la consola y sus mandos, incluyendo la iconografía del triángulo, el cuadrado, el círculo y la X -la simbología de un punto de vista, un trozo de papel, y las decisiones sí y no, respectivamente-, a Teiyu Goto le llega el reto de diseñar PS2 . Sobre el papel, un concepto que el propio diseñador aún mantiene entre sus logros más destacados en su página web : “ transmitir hacia el oscuro espacio exterior desde nuestro planeta de agua lleno de inteligencia ”. ¿El resultado? El clásico monolito negro con tintes azules que todos conocemos. Las comparaciones, como ya habréis podido comprobar por las imágenes, ceden hueco a mucho más que una bonita casualidad. Pese a los cambios estéticos, la similitud entre el ordenador de Atari y PS2 es más que evidente. Y lo es por razones justificadas, al menos a nivel legal, tal y como muestra esta patente . De aquella hecatombe que supuso el lanzamiento de Jaguar y la caída de Atari , Sony supo sacar tajada adquiriendo aquél diseño a la espera de darle una segunda vida. El mundo se quedó sin su Falcon 040, pero la suerte quiso que aquella idea volviese a la vida con el diseño de PS2 .
